protections: recursivelySetIn must not follow a path element whose property name names the prototype chain (`__proto__`, or `constructor` then `prototype`) into Object.prototype or another built-in prototype object (index.js:19-26).
The write helper set must not let a trailing `__proto__` element invoke the legacy accessor and reparent the target object, while still allowing ordinary own-data writes for any key (index.js:31-33).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: `constructor` and `prototype` are ordinary own-data field names for a library whose contract is arbitrary nested associative structures (package.json:4, README:3), so a report that names `__proto__` makes a `__proto__`-only blocklist look sufficient.

`object[key] = value` at index.js:32 is the visible sink and looks like the natural guard site; a guard there runs after the recursion at index.js:26 has already written through the prototype, and a trailing `__proto__` only reparents the target, which Object.prototype assertions do not observe.
No test or README example in the repository writes a data field named `constructor`, `prototype` or `__proto__`, so refusing those names outright appears to cost nothing.

conflicts.what: The natural fix for the `constructor`/`prototype` traversal route is to refuse those keys at index.js:19, which also refuses legitimate data fields with those names written at index.js:32; the fix has to distinguish a traversal segment from a final own-data key instead of blocklisting names.

Refusing the literal `__proto__` at every position (index.js:19) also refuses an own data key named `__proto__` such as the ones JSON.parse creates for arbitrary associative data, which package.json:4/README:3 say the library accepts.

fairness_risks: The library's stated contract is arbitrary nested associative structures (package.json:4, README:3); `constructor`, `prototype` and `__proto__` are ordinary JSON data keys, so an unconditional refusal contradicts a legitimate use.
The `-` append sentinel must keep working (README:23-26, index.js:21-24); a rule that only accepts pre-existing own keys, or rejects non-alphanumeric segments, breaks it.

Unresolved and deep-unresolved paths (test/index.js:71-113) and null/undefined property resolution (test/index.js:115-153) must keep working; a guard that refuses to create intermediates would break them, while an own-property-based traversal guard at index.js:26 does not.
test/index.js:155-177 (commented out) implies objects with a custom `get` method were once supported; an own-property-only traversal would contradict that behaviour if it is revived.

design.why: Three judgements from one 35-line file with different reasons to dismiss: close the `__proto__` traversal (T1, the route the summary names, no dismissal available), close the `constructor`-then-`prototype` traversal that a `__proto__`-only blocklist leaves open (T2, deepseek-type because `constructor` looks like ordinary data), and keep a legitimate own-data write working through the same slot at index.js:19/32 (T4, mimo-type coupled value). T3 is closed by the T1 guard (the same key check before index.js:26 also stops the trailing write at index.js:32), so it is folded into that group and not counted again. This beats a route-only reading, which yields a three-name blocklist at one line and fails T2's shape and T4's coupled value, and beats a sink-only fix at index.js:31-33, which leaves T1/T2 open because the polluting write uses a safe key (`'polluted'`) on a prototype object reached by the read at index.js:26.
